title: Ἀθηνᾶ ἐν Λακεδαίμονι
about: Athena goes to Sparta and finds Telemachus awake with worry beside the sleeping Peisistratus in the vestibule of Menelaus's house. She tells him to leave at once: his mother is being urged to marry Eurymachus, who outdoes the other suitors in gifts, and a band of suitors is lying in ambush for him in the strait between Ithaca and Same. He must keep clear of the islands, sail by night, and on reaching Ithaca go first to the swineherd. Telemachus wakes Peisistratus, who says they must wait for dawn and for Menelaus's gifts. At dawn Menelaus comes, Telemachus asks to be sent home, and Menelaus agrees: a host should neither hold back nor hurry a guest. He offers to take him on a journey through Hellas and Argos and to give him a gift at every stop.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ εἰς εὐρύχορον Λακεδαίμονα Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
ᾤχετ’, Ὀδυσσῆος μεγαθύμου φαίδιμον υἱὸν
νόστου ὑπομνήσουσα καὶ ὀτρυνέουσα νέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
And she to Lacedaemon, of wide dancing-grounds, Pallas Athena
went, great-hearted Odysseus' glorious son
of homecoming to remind, and to urge to return.
sentences.i: Pallas Athena went to spacious Lacedaemon, to remind the glorious son of great-hearted Odysseus of his homecoming and to urge him to return.
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is 'and she': in Homer the old article is a pronoun, and here it picks Athena up as the subject. ᾤχετ’ is the imperfect of οἴχομαι 'be gone, go off'. ὑπομνήσουσα and ὀτρυνέουσα are future participles that give purpose: she went 'to remind' and 'to urge'; ὑπομιμνήσκω takes the person in the accusative (Ὀδυσσῆος … υἱόν) and the thing in the genitive (νόστου). μεγάθυμος is 'great-hearted' and φαίδιμος 'glorious'. εὐρύχορον, literally 'of wide dancing-grounds', is the epithet of Lacedaemon; the English says 'spacious'. The meaning of Παλλάς, Athena's second name, is disputed.

sentences.t:
εὗρε δὲ Τηλέμαχον καὶ Νέστορος ἀγλαὸν υἱὸν
εὕδοντ’ ἐν προδόμῳ Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο,
ἦ τοι Νεστορίδην μαλακῷ δεδμημένον ὕπνῳ·
sentences.i: She found Telemachus and the splendid son of Nestor asleep in the vestibule of glorious Menelaus; the son of Nestor, indeed, was overcome by soft sleep;
sentences.n: εὗρε, the unaugmented aorist of εὑρίσκω, has two objects, Τηλέμαχον and Νέστορος … υἱόν; εὕδοντ’ is the dual participle (εὕδοντε, elided) 'the two sleeping'. The second is Peisistratus, who is named at 46; ἀγλαός is 'splendid'. The πρόδομος is the room or porch in front of the main hall: 'fore-house' in the literal layer, 'vestibule' in the other. Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο is a genitive in -οιο, 'of glorious Menelaus'. Νεστορίδην is a patronymic, 'son of Nestor', and ἦ τοι sets him against Telemachus in the next unit. δεδμημένον is the perfect passive participle of δάμνημι 'overpower': he is overcome by sleep.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχον δ’ οὐχ ὕπνος ἔχε γλυκύς, ἀλλ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην μελεδήματα πατρὸς ἔγειρεν.
sentences.l:
But Telemachus not sleep held, sweet, but in his heart
through the ambrosial night cares for his father kept rousing him.
sentences.i: But sweet sleep did not hold Telemachus; in his heart, all through the ambrosial night, cares for his father kept him wakeful.
sentences.n: Τηλέμαχον is the object, 'Telemachus sleep did not hold': ἔχε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω, and γλυκύς 'sweet' follows its noun. νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην is 'through the ambrosial night': δι’ is διά with the accusative, and ἀμβρόσιος is 'deathless, divine', from the root of ἄμβροτος. μελεδήματα, 'cares', is related to μέλω 'be a care', and πατρός is an objective genitive: cares for his father. ἔγειρεν 'was rousing' has the cares as its subject; the poet uses the same verb of Telemachus waking Peisistratus at 44.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: And standing close by addressed him gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Gleaming-eyed Athena came and stood close beside him, and said to him:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη is 'and standing close by', the participle of ἵσταμαι, and προσέφη is 'addressed': the pair is a speech introduction, and the speech begins in the next unit. The Greek has no quotation marks; the English adds them. γλαυκῶπις is Athena's stock epithet, translated every time: 'gleaming-eyed', from γλαυκός 'gleaming'.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, οὐκέτι καλὰ δόμων ἄπο τῆλ’ ἀλάλησαι,
κτήματά τε προλιπὼν ἄνδρας τ’ ἐν σοῖσι δόμοισιν
οὕτω ὑπερφιάλους·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, no longer finely, away from home, far off, do you wander,
leaving behind both your possessions and men in your house
so overbearing,
sentences.i: “Telemachus, it is no longer well that you wander far from home, leaving your possessions behind and men so overbearing in your house,
sentences.n: Τηλέμαχ’ is the vocative with the final vowel elided. ἀλάλησαι is a perfect of ἀλάομαι 'wander' with a present sense, 'you are wandering', and οὐκέτι καλά, 'no longer finely', is mild for 'this is not good'. δόμων ἄπο is 'from home' with ἄπο after its noun and so accented; τῆλε 'far off'. ὑπερφιάλους, said of the men left in the house, means 'overbearing', as at 3.315. The unit ends at Murray’s stop after ὑπερφιάλους; the fear clause μή τοι … follows in the next unit. Lines 11–13 repeat 3.314–316 (12 has φάγωσι for φάγωσιν, in the next unit), and line 10 ends like 3.313, with ἀλάλησαι for ἀλάλησο.

sentences.t:
μή τοι κατὰ πάντα φάγωσι
κτήματα δασσάμενοι, σὺ δὲ τηϋσίην ὁδὸν ἔλθῃς.
sentences.l:
lest they eat up everything,
having divided your possessions, and you go a fruitless journey.
sentences.i: for fear that they eat up everything, dividing your possessions among them, and that you make a fruitless journey.
sentences.n: μή τοι κατὰ πάντα φάγωσι is a fear clause hanging on the last unit: ‘lest they eat up everything’, with κατὰ … φάγωσι tmesis for καταφάγωσι, an aorist subjunctive. κτήματα δασσάμενοι: δασσάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of δατέομαι ‘divide among themselves’. σὺ δὲ … ἔλθῃς is still under μή, a subjunctive of ἔρχομαι: ‘lest … you go’. τηϋσίην is ‘fruitless, in vain’ and agrees with ὁδόν ‘journey’. The unit begins mid-line 12, after Murray’s stop. The rest of line 12 and line 13 are also 3.315–316.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὄτρυνε τάχιστα βοὴν ἀγαθὸν Μενέλαον
πεμπέμεν, ὄφρ’ ἔτι οἴκοι ἀμύμονα μητέρα τέτμῃς.
sentences.l:
But urge, as quickly as possible, Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
to send you off, so that still at home your blameless mother you may find.
sentences.i: But urge Menelaus, good at the war-cry, to send you on your way as quickly as possible, so that you may still find your blameless mother at home.
sentences.n: ὄτρυνε is the imperative of ὀτρύνω 'urge on', the verb that appears again as an infinitive at 37 and 40. πεμπέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, 'to send you off', and the object 'you' is left out. τάχιστα is the superlative adverb, 'as quickly as possible'. βοὴν ἀγαθός, Menelaus's epithet, is 'good at the war-cry': βοήν is an accusative of respect. ὄφρα with the subjunctive τέτμῃς (from τέτμον 'come upon, find') gives purpose. ἀμύμονα is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known; 'blameless' is the traditional guess. οἴκοι is 'at home'.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ ῥα πατήρ τε κασίγνητοί τε κέλονται
Εὐρυμάχῳ γήμασθαι·
sentences.l:
For already, indeed, both her father and her brothers urge
her to marry Eurymachus;
sentences.i: For already her father and her brothers are urging her to marry Eurymachus;
sentences.n: The person urged is not named: the 'mother' of line 15 is meant. γήμασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of γαμέω 'marry', said of a woman 'to take a husband', and Εὐρυμάχῳ is the dative 'Eurymachus'. κέλονται 'they urge' takes the infinitive. τε … τε is 'both … and', and ῥα is the particle 'then, so'. Her father and brothers are mentioned only here in this part.

sentences.t:
ὁ γὰρ περιβάλλει ἅπαντας
μνηστῆρας δώροισι καὶ ἐξώφελλεν ἔεδνα·
sentences.l:
for he surpasses all
the suitors in gifts, and was increasing the bridal gifts;
sentences.i: for he surpasses all the suitors in gifts, and has been adding to the bridal gifts;
sentences.n: ὁ is 'he', Eurymachus. περιβάλλει is literally 'throws round' and means 'surpass': the accusative ἅπαντας μνηστῆρας is the people outdone and the dative δώροισι (-οισι) the respect, 'in gifts'. ἐξώφελλεν is the imperfect of ἐξοφέλλω 'increase greatly', from ὀφέλλω, which Athena uses again at 21. ἔεδνα, a form of ἕεδνα, are bridal gifts, given by a suitor to the bride's family. The imperfect shows the adding still going on.

sentences.t: μή νύ τι σεῦ ἀέκητι δόμων ἐκ κτῆμα φέρηται.
sentences.l: lest in any way, against your will, from the house a possession she carry off.
sentences.i: so that she may not carry off any possession from the house against your will.
sentences.n: μή with the subjunctive φέρηται is 'lest'; νύ is 'now' and τι 'at all'. σεῦ ἀέκητι is 'against your will' with the genitive. ἐκ … δόμων is 'out of the house'. φέρηται is middle, 'carry off for herself', and its unstated subject is the mother. κτῆμα is the singular of κτήματα (11, 13).

sentences.t: οἶσθα γὰρ οἷος θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι γυναικός·
sentences.l: For you know what kind of heart is in the breast of a woman:
sentences.i: For you know what kind of heart a woman has in her breast:
sentences.n: οἶσθα is 'you know' (οἶδα). οἷος is 'what kind of', so 'you know what sort of heart …'. στήθεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, 'in the breast'. The ano teleia leads into the saying of the next unit, which is stated of women in general.

sentences.t:
κείνου βούλεται οἶκον ὀφέλλειν ὅς κεν ὀπυίῃ,
παίδων δὲ προτέρων καὶ κουριδίοιο φίλοιο
οὐκέτι μέμνηται τεθνηκότος οὐδὲ μεταλλᾷ.
sentences.l:
of that man she wants the house to increase, whoever may marry her,
but of her earlier children and of her wedded dear one
no longer is she mindful, now dead, nor does she inquire.
sentences.i: She wants to increase the house of whoever marries her, and no longer remembers her earlier children, or the dear husband she wedded, now dead, nor asks after them.
sentences.n: κείνου is Ionic ἐκείνου, 'of that man', and ὅς κεν ὀπυίῃ is a general relative, 'whoever may take her as wife' (ὀπυίω, subjunctive). οἶκον ὀφέλλειν is 'to increase the house'. κουριδίοιο is a genitive in -οιο of κουρίδιος 'wedded, lawful', and φίλοιο is 'dear'. μέμνηται (μιμνήσκομαι) takes the genitives παίδων and κουριδίοιο φίλοιο, with τεθνηκότος 'of the dead one' agreeing with the husband; μεταλλᾷ (μεταλλάω 'inquire') has the same objects understood. The Greek states it as a rule about women, not about a particular woman.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ ἐλθὼν αὐτὸς ἐπιτρέψειας ἕκαστα
δμῳάων ἥ τίς τοι ἀρίστη φαίνεται εἶναι,
εἰς ὅ κέ τοι φήνωσι θεοὶ κυδρὴν παράκοιτιν.
sentences.l:
But you yourself, having come, may entrust each thing
to one of the maidservants, whichever seems to you to be best,
until the gods show you a glorious wife.
sentences.i: But when you are home, entrust everything yourself to whichever of the maids seems to you the best, until the gods show you a glorious wife.
sentences.n: ἐπιτρέψειας is an optative (aorist of ἐπιτρέπω) used as a polite command, 'do entrust'. ἕκαστα is 'each thing', that is the whole household. δμῳάων is the genitive plural (Attic δμῳῶν) of δμῳή 'maidservant', partitive after ἥ τίς: ἥ τίς τοι ἀρίστη φαίνεται εἶναι is 'whichever seems to you to be best'. εἰς ὅ κε with the subjunctive φήνωσι is 'until they show'. κυδρήν is 'glorious', and παράκοιτις 'wife' is literally 'one who lies beside'.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοί τι ἔπος ἐρέω, σὺ δὲ σύνθεο θυμῷ.
sentences.l: And another word to you I shall say, and you, lay it to heart.
sentences.i: I have another word to tell you, and you must lay it to heart.
sentences.n: ἐρέω is the future 'I shall say' (Attic ἐρῶ), and τοί is 'to you'. σύνθεο is the aorist middle imperative of συντίθημι 'put together', so 'take it in, lay it to heart'; θυμῷ is 'heart'. The word that follows is the warning about the ambush.

sentences.t:
μνηστήρων σ’ ἐπιτηδὲς ἀριστῆες λοχόωσιν
ἐν πορθμῷ Ἰθάκης τε Σάμοιό τε παιπαλοέσσης.
sentences.l:
Of the suitors you purposely the best men are lying in ambush for
in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Same.
sentences.i: The best men among the suitors are lying in ambush for you on purpose, in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Same.
sentences.n: μνηστήρων depends on ἀριστῆες 'the best men of the suitors'; σ’ is σε, the object of λοχόωσιν, a stretched form of λοχάω 'lie in ambush for'. ἐπιτηδές is 'on purpose'. πορθμός is 'strait, crossing'. Σάμοιο is a genitive in -οιο, and Σάμος is Same, here an island by Ithaca; παιπαλοέσσης is 'rugged'. Line 29 is word for word 4.671.

sentences.t: ἱέμενοι κτεῖναι, πρὶν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l: eager to kill you, before you reach your fatherland.
sentences.i: eager to kill you before you reach your native land.
sentences.n: ἱέμενοι is the middle participle of ἵημι 'be eager, press on', agreeing with the suitors of the line before; the same word at 69 is said of Telemachus. κτεῖναι is the aorist infinitive of κτείνω 'kill', and πρίν with the infinitive is 'before'. πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'fatherland', the land of one's father. The line is word for word 4.823.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τά γ’ οὐκ ὀΐω·
sentences.l: But that I do not think will be;
sentences.i: But I do not think that will happen;
sentences.n: τά γε is 'that', the ambush, and ὀΐω is the first person of ὀΐομαι 'think, suppose'. οὐκ ὀΐω is 'I do not expect it'. The ano teleia is Murray's, and the reason Athena gives follows in the next unit.

sentences.t:
πρὶν καί τινα γαῖα καθέξει
ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων, οἵ τοι βίοτον κατέδουσιν.
sentences.l:
before the earth will hold down some
of the men, the suitors, who eat up your livelihood.
sentences.i: Before it does, the earth will hold down some of the suitors who are eating up your livelihood.
sentences.n: καθέξει is the future of κατέχω, 'will hold down', after πρίν, and γαῖα is the earth, which holds the dead. καί goes with τινα 'even some'. ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων is 'of the men, the suitors', a genitive of the group. οἵ τοι βίοτον κατέδουσιν is 'who eat up your livelihood': κατέδουσιν is κατεσθίω, and βίοτον is 'means of life'. The line 32 stands twice in Book 13, at 396 and 428; line 31 is 13.427.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ἑκὰς νήσων ἀπέχειν εὐεργέα νῆα,
νυκτὶ δ’ ὁμῶς πλείειν·
sentences.l:
But far from the islands keep your well-made ship,
and by night, equally, sail;
sentences.i: But keep your well-made ship far away from the islands, and sail by night as well as by day;
sentences.n: The infinitives ἀπέχειν and πλείειν are used as commands, 'keep' and 'sail', as Homer often does. ἑκάς is 'far' and takes the genitive νήσων 'from the islands'. εὐεργέα is the accusative of εὐεργής 'well-made'. νυκτὶ ὁμῶς is 'by night equally', that is, as by day: the dative gives the time. πλείειν is the Homeric infinitive of πλέω 'sail' (Attic πλεῖν). The islands are not named here.

sentences.t:
πέμψει δέ τοι οὖρον ὄπισθεν
ἀθανάτων ὅς τίς σε φυλάσσει τε ῥύεταί τε.
sentences.l:
and he will send you a fair wind from behind,
of the immortals whoever guards you and protects you.
sentences.i: and one of the immortals who guards and protects you will send you a fair wind from behind.
sentences.n: The subject of πέμψει 'will send' is the relative clause ὅς τίς … 'whoever', a god Athena does not name; ἀθανάτων 'of the immortals' is a partitive genitive. The object is οὖρον 'fair wind', and ὄπισθεν 'from behind'. φυλάσσει and ῥύεται (ῥύομαι 'protect') make a pair joined by τε … τε.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν πρώτην ἀκτὴν Ἰθάκης ἀφίκηαι,
νῆα μὲν ἐς πόλιν ὀτρῦναι καὶ πάντας ἑταίρους,
αὐτὸς δὲ πρώτιστα συβώτην εἰσαφικέσθαι,
ὅς τοι ὑῶν ἐπίουρος, ὁμῶς δέ τοι ἤπια οἶδεν.
sentences.l:
But when the first shore of Ithaca you reach,
the ship, indeed, to the city urge on, and all your companions,
and you yourself, first of all, to the swineherd go,
who is guardian of the swine, and likewise kindly things knows for you.
sentences.i: But when you reach the first shore of Ithaca, send your ship on to the city with all your companions, and you yourself must first of all go to the swineherd, who watches over the swine and is likewise kindly disposed to you.
sentences.n: ἐπήν is ἐπεί + ἄν 'when', with the subjunctive ἀφίκηαι (the epic ending -ηαι for -ῃ), so 'whenever you arrive'. The infinitives ὀτρῦναι and εἰσαφικέσθαι are commands again. ἀκτή is 'shore' or 'headland', and πρώτην 'first'. νῆα μέν … αὐτὸς δέ sets the ship against the man: the ship goes to the city, he himself first to the swineherd. συβώτης 'swineherd' is a common noun here. ὑῶν is the genitive plural of ὗς 'swine', with ἐπίουρος 'guardian'. ἤπια is the neuter plural of ἤπιος 'kindly', and ἤπια οἶδεν, 'knows kindly things', means 'is kindly disposed'. Lines 38–39 are 13.404–405 (39 has οἶδεν where 13.405 has οἶδε).

sentences.t: ἔνθα δὲ νύκτ’ ἀέσαι·
sentences.l: And there pass the night;
sentences.i: and spend the night there;
sentences.n: ἀέσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἄω, a verb 'pass the night, sleep', again used as a command. νύκτ’ is an accusative of time: 'pass the night'. ἔνθα is 'there', at the swineherd's. The unit is short because Murray's ano teleia closes it.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὀτρῦναι πόλιν εἴσω
ἀγγελίην ἐρέοντα περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ,
οὕνεκά οἱ σῶς ἐσσὶ καὶ ἐκ Πύλου εἰλήλουθας.
sentences.l:
and him urge on, into the city,
a message to tell to circumspect Penelope,
that for her safe you are, and from Pylos have come.”
sentences.i: and send him on into the city to take the news to circumspect Penelope, that you are safe and have come back from Pylos.”
sentences.n: τόν is 'him', the swineherd, and ὀτρῦναι is a third command infinitive, 'urge on, send'. ἐρέοντα is the future participle of ἐρέω 'I shall say', here expressing purpose, 'to tell', with ἀγγελίην 'message' as its object. Πηνελοπείῃ is the dative of Πηνελόπεια; περίφρων 'circumspect' is her standing epithet. οὕνεκα, the same as ὅτι, introduces what the message is, and οἱ is 'for her'. σῶς ἐσσί is 'you are safe' (ἐσσί is the old form of εἶ), and εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι 'have come'. The closing quotation mark ends Athena's speech.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη πρὸς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον,
αὐτὰρ ὁ Νεστορίδην ἐξ ἡδέος ὕπνου ἔγειρεν
λὰξ ποδὶ κινήσας, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
She, indeed, then so having spoken went away to tall Olympus,
but he the son of Nestor from sweet sleep roused,
with a kick, with his foot, having stirred him, and to him a speech uttered:
sentences.i: So she spoke and went away to tall Olympus, and he woke the son of Nestor from sweet sleep, stirring him with a kick of his foot, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: ἡ μέν … αὐτὰρ ὁ is 'she, on the one hand … but he': ὁ is Telemachus, now the subject, and the Greek does not name him. εἰποῦσ’ is the aorist participle of εἶπον 'say', elided, and ἀπέβη 'went away'. μακρόν is 'tall' here. Νεστορίδην is 'the son of Nestor', and ἔγειρεν 'woke', is the verb of line 8. λάξ is 'with the heel, by kicking', and κινήσας 'having stirred'. πρὸς … ἔειπεν is tmesis for προσέειπεν, and μῦθον is 'a speech': the speech follows in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἔγρεο, Νεστορίδη Πεισίστρατε, μώνυχας ἵππους
ζεῦξον ὑφ’ ἅρματ’ ἄγων, ὄφρα πρήσσωμεν ὁδοῖο.
sentences.l:
“Wake up, son of Nestor, Peisistratus, solid-hoofed horses
yoke beneath the chariot, leading them, so that we may make headway on our road.”
sentences.i: “Wake up, Peisistratus, son of Nestor, and bring the solid-hoofed horses and yoke them to the chariot, so that we may make headway on our road.”
sentences.n: ἔγρεο is the aorist middle imperative of ἐγείρω, 'wake up'. Νεστορίδη Πεισίστρατε are both vocative. μώνυχας is 'solid-hoofed', from μώνυξ 'with a single, undivided hoof', the stock epithet of horses. ζεῦξον is the aorist imperative of ζεύγνυμι 'yoke', and ὑφ’ ἅρματ’ is ὑπό with the accusative, 'under the chariot', to which the horses are yoked; ἄγων is 'leading, bringing' the horses up. ὄφρα with the subjunctive πρήσσωμεν gives purpose, and πρήσσω ὁδοῖο is 'make headway on the road' with a partitive genitive: 'get some of the road done'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Νεστορίδης Πεισίστρατος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: Him then in turn spoke Peisistratus, Nestor's son, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Peisistratus, son of Nestor, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This reply-formula is the same line as 4.155: τόν is 'him', Telemachus, and αὖ 'in turn'. Νεστορίδης is the patronymic 'son of Nestor' and Πεισίστρατος the name. ἀντίον is 'face to face', and ηὔδα, the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak', has its augment contracted into ηὐ-. The speech follows.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, οὔ πως ἔστιν ἐπειγομένους περ ὁδοῖο
νύκτα διὰ δνοφερὴν ἐλάαν·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, in no way is it possible, though eager for the road,
through the gloomy night to drive;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, there is no way for us to drive on through the gloomy night, however eager we are for the road;
sentences.n: οὔ πως ἔστιν is 'there is in no way (it is not possible)', followed by the infinitive ἐλάαν, a stretched form of ἐλαύνειν 'drive'. ἐπειγομένους is accusative, agreeing with the unspoken 'us', with περ 'even though', and ὁδοῖο is a genitive, 'eager for the road'. In νύκτα διὰ δνοφερήν the preposition stands between noun and adjective; δνοφερός is 'gloomy, dark', Peisistratus's word for the night's darkness. The plural shows he speaks for both of them.

sentences.t: τάχα δ’ ἔσσεται ἠώς.
sentences.l: and soon there will be dawn.
sentences.i: and dawn will soon come.
sentences.n: ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί 'will be' (Attic ἔσται), with the σ doubled; ἠώς is 'dawn'. τάχα is 'soon, presently' (the Attic sense 'perhaps' is a later one). The clause gives the reason for waiting.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μέν’ εἰς ὅ κε δῶρα φέρων ἐπιδίφρια θήῃ
ἥρως Ἀτρείδης, δουρικλειτὸς Μενέλαος,
καὶ μύθοις ἀγανοῖσι παραυδήσας ἀποπέμψῃ.
sentences.l:
But wait until, gifts bringing, for the chariot-seat he puts them,
the hero, Atreus' son, Menelaus famed-for-the-spear,
and with gentle words having spoken soothingly he sends us off.
sentences.i: But wait until the hero Menelaus, son of Atreus, famed for his spear, has brought gifts and put them on the chariot, and has spoken soothingly to us with gentle words and sent us on our way.
sentences.n: μέν’ is the imperative μένε 'wait'. εἰς ὅ κε with the subjunctives θήῃ and ἀποπέμψῃ is 'until he has put … and sent'. ἐπιδίφρια δῶρα is 'gifts for the chariot', gifts to lie on the chariot-seat (ἐπὶ δίφρον). ἥρως Ἀτρείδης is 'the hero, the son of Atreus', and Ἀτρείδης is the patronymic used again at 64. δουρικλειτός is 'famed for the spear' (δόρυ 'spear' + κλειτός 'famous'). μύθοις ἀγανοῖσι is 'with gentle words', and παραυδήσας 'having spoken soothingly'. Menelaus is the subject throughout.

sentences.t:
τοῦ γάρ τε ξεῖνος μιμνήσκεται ἤματα πάντα
ἀνδρὸς ξεινοδόκου, ὅς κεν φιλότητα παράσχῃ.
sentences.l:
For of him the guest-friend is mindful all his days,
of the man who receives guests, whoever may offer friendship.”
sentences.i: For a guest-friend remembers all his days a host, whoever offers him friendship.”
sentences.n: τοῦ … ἀνδρὸς ξεινοδόκου is 'of him, the man who receives guests': μιμνήσκεται 'is mindful' takes the genitive, and the noun is held back to the next line. The τε of γάρ τε is the epic τε that marks a general truth: this is a saying, not a statement about one man. ξεῖνος is the 'guest-friend', tied by hospitality, and ξεινοδόκος is 'receiving guests'. ἤματα πάντα is 'all his days'. ὅς κεν … παράσχῃ is 'whoever may offer', with φιλότητα 'friendship'. The closing quotation mark ends Peisistratus's speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτίκα δὲ χρυσόθρονος ἤλυθεν Ἠώς.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and golden-throned Dawn came at once.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is the elided ὣς ἔφατο, 'so (he) spoke', the formula that closes a speech; the speaker here is Peisistratus, so read 'he'. The English says 'she' because this line repeats 10.541 word for word and the published English of that line is kept. χρυσόθρονος is 'golden-throned'; an old alternative derives the second part from θρόνα 'embroidered flowers', so the sense is not quite certain. ἤλυθεν is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἦλθεν). Dawn comes as Peisistratus predicted at 50.

sentences.t:
ἀγχίμολον δέ σφ’ ἦλθε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος,
ἀνστὰς ἐξ εὐνῆς, Ἑλένης πάρα καλλικόμοιο.
sentences.l:
And close by them came Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
having risen from his bed, from beside Helen of the fair hair.
sentences.i: Menelaus, good at the war-cry, came near them, having risen from his bed beside Helen of the fair hair.
sentences.n: ἀγχίμολον is an adverb 'close by', and σφ’ is σφε, 'them'. ἀνστάς is the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, 'having risen'. εὐνή is the bed, here the marriage-bed. Ἑλένης πάρα is 'from beside Helen' with πάρα after its noun and so accented. καλλικόμοιο is a genitive in -οιο, 'of the fair hair' (καλλι- 'fair' + κόμη 'hair'), Helen's epithet.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός,
σπερχόμενός ῥα χιτῶνα περὶ χροῒ σιγαλόεντα
δῦνεν,
sentences.l:
And him when then he noticed, Odysseus' dear son,
hurrying, then, a tunic about his skin, glossy,
he put on,
sentences.i: When the dear son of Odysseus noticed him, he hurried to put on a glossy tunic over his skin,
sentences.n: τόν is 'him', Menelaus. ὡς οὖν ἐνόησεν is 'when then he noticed', with the aorist of νοέω 'perceive'. Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός is Telemachus, whose name does not come until line 63. σπερχόμενος is 'hurrying', and ῥα the particle 'then'. χιτών is the tunic, and περὶ χροΐ, 'about the skin', puts it next to the body (χροΐ is the dative of χρώς). σιγαλόεντα 'glossy' agrees with χιτῶνα. δῦνεν is the unaugmented imperfect of δύνω 'put on'; the sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
καὶ μέγα φᾶρος ἐπὶ στιβαροῖς βάλετ’ ὤμοις
ἥρως, βῆ δὲ θύραζε, παριστάμενος δὲ προσηύδα
Τηλέμαχος, φίλος υἱὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο·
sentences.l:
and a great cloak upon his stout shoulders he threw,
the hero, and he went to the door, and standing beside him spoke
Telemachus, dear son of Odysseus, divine:
sentences.i: and the hero threw a great cloak over his stout shoulders and went toward the door; and, standing beside him, Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus, spoke to him:
sentences.n: φᾶρος is a man's cloak, thrown over the tunic; βάλετ’ is the unaugmented aorist middle of βάλλω, 'threw upon himself', with ἐπὶ στιβαροῖς ὤμοις 'upon his stout shoulders'. στιβαροῖς is 'stout'. ἥρως, 'the hero', is a title, and Τηλέμαχος in line 63 is in apposition to it: the name comes last. βῆ δὲ θύραζε is 'and he went to the door' (-ζε marks direction). παριστάμενος is 'standing beside', and προσηύδα 'spoke to'. θείοιο is the genitive of θεῖος 'divine' and belongs to Ὀδυσσῆος.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
ἤδη νῦν μ’ ἀπόπεμπε φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.l:
“Atreus' son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people,
already now send me away to my dear fatherland;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people, send me away now to my dear fatherland;
sentences.n: The first line is the same address as 4.156, there spoken to Menelaus by Peisistratus. Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative of the patronymic; διοτρεφές 'Zeus-nurtured' and ὄρχαμε λαῶν 'chief of the people' are stock honours for a king. ἀπόπεμπε is the present imperative 'send away'. φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'to my dear fatherland', with ἐς for εἰς. ἤδη νῦν is 'already now', that is 'now at last'.

sentences.t: ἤδη γάρ μοι θυμὸς ἐέλδεται οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l: for already to me my heart longs homeward to come.”
sentences.i: for my heart already longs to reach home.”
sentences.n: ἐέλδεται is 'longs', from ἐέλδομαι 'desire'. It takes the infinitive οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι: οἴκαδε is 'homeward', with the -δε of direction, and ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι 'reach'. μοι θυμός is 'my heart', the seat of wishing. The closing quotation mark ends Telemachus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: Him then answered Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Then Menelaus, good at the war-cry, answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is the formula 'Him then answered': ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι 'answer', and ἔπειτα 'then'. βοὴν ἀγαθός, 'good at the war-cry', is Menelaus's standing epithet: βοή is the battle-shout, in an accusative of respect. The speech begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, οὔ τί σ’ ἐγώ γε πολὺν χρόνον ἐνθάδ’ ἐρύξω
ἱέμενον νόστοιο·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, in no way will I keep you for a long time here,
eager for homecoming;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, I will not keep you here for long, eager as you are for your homecoming;
sentences.n: ἐρύξω is the future of ἐρύκω 'hold back, detain', with σε as object and πολὺν χρόνον 'for a long time' as an accusative of duration. οὔ τί is 'in no way' (τι an adverb), and γε 'for my part'. ἱέμενον, a middle participle of ἵημι, agrees with σε, 'eager for', and νόστοιο is the genitive it takes ('homecoming', -οιο). Compare ἱέμενοι in line 30, the suitors eager to kill.

sentences.t:
νεμεσσῶμαι δὲ καὶ ἄλλῳ
ἀνδρὶ ξεινοδόκῳ, ὅς κ’ ἔξοχα μὲν φιλέῃσιν,
ἔξοχα δ’ ἐχθαίρῃσιν·
sentences.i: and I also take offence at any other host who welcomes beyond measure, or hates beyond measure;
sentences.n: νεμεσσῶμαι is 'I take offence at', from νεμεσάω, the feeling at seeing what is improper, and it takes the dative ἄλλῳ ἀνδρὶ ξεινοδόκῳ 'another man, a host'; καί is 'also'. ὅς κ’ … φιλέῃσιν and ἐχθαίρῃσιν are general relative clauses, κεν with subjunctives in -ῃσιν. φιλέω said of a host is 'welcome', ἐχθαίρω is 'hate'. ἔξοχα is 'beyond others, beyond measure'. The ano teleia leads to the saying of the next unit.

sentences.t: ἀμείνω δ’ αἴσιμα πάντα.
sentences.l: but better are all things done in due measure.
sentences.i: and better is everything done in due measure.
sentences.n: ἀμείνω is the contracted neuter plural of ἀμείνων 'better' (ἀμείνονα). αἴσιμα is the neuter plural 'in due measure', from αἶσα 'due portion'. The words are a general saying, and the next lines apply it to the two kinds of fault in a host.

sentences.t:
ἶσόν τοι κακόν ἐσθ’, ὅς τ’ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα νέεσθαι
ξεῖνον ἐποτρύνει καὶ ὃς ἐσσύμενον κατερύκει.
sentences.l:
An equal evil it is, whoever a guest-friend not willing to go
urges on, and whoever holds back one hastening.
sentences.i: It is an equal evil, you see, to urge a guest-friend on his way when he does not wish to go, and to hold back one who is in haste.
sentences.n: ἶσον is the neuter 'equal'; τοι is 'you see'; κακόν 'an evil' is the predicate, and ἐσθ’ is ἐστί. ὅς τ’ … ἐποτρύνει and καὶ ὃς … κατερύκει are two general relative clauses, 'whoever urges … and whoever holds back'. ἐθέλοντα and ἐσσύμενον ('hastening', from σεύομαι) agree with ξεῖνον, 'a guest-friend', the one who has a tie of hospitality. νέεσθαι is the uncontracted infinitive 'to go, to go home'.

sentences.t: χρὴ ξεῖνον παρεόντα φιλεῖν, ἐθέλοντα δὲ πέμπειν.
sentences.l: One must welcome a guest-friend while he is present, and send him on when he is willing.
sentences.i: A host ought to welcome a guest-friend while he is there, and to send him on his way when he wishes to go.
sentences.n: χρή is 'it is necessary' and takes accusative and infinitive: ξεῖνον is the object of both φιλεῖν 'to welcome' and πέμπειν 'to send on his way'. παρεόντα, 'being present', and ἐθέλοντα, 'being willing (to go)', are participles agreeing with ξεῖνον. The line sums up the two faults of 72–73 as one rule.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μέν’ εἰς ὅ κε δῶρα φέρων ἐπιδίφρια θείω
καλά, σὺ δ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδῃς, εἴπω δὲ γυναιξὶ
δεῖπνον ἐνὶ μεγάροις τετυκεῖν ἅλις ἔνδον ἐόντων.
sentences.l:
But wait until, gifts bringing, for the chariot-seat I put them,
fine ones, and you with your eyes see them, and I tell the women
a meal in the halls to prepare, enough from what is within.
sentences.i: But wait until I have brought fine gifts and put them on the chariot, and you have seen them with your own eyes, and I have told the women to prepare a meal in the halls, enough from what is in the house.
sentences.n: Line 75 is line 51 with θείω, 'I put' (a subjunctive of τίθημι), for θήῃ 'he puts'. εἰς ὅ κε takes three subjunctives, θείω, ἴδῃς 'you see' and εἴπω 'I tell'. καλά 'fine' agrees with δῶρα. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, 'with your own eyes'. τετυκεῖν is the aorist infinitive of τεύχω 'make ready', and with δεῖπνον 'a meal' it follows εἴπω, 'tell the women to prepare'. ἅλις is 'enough', and ἔνδον ἐόντων is 'of what is within', a partitive genitive plural: enough from what is in the house. μεγάροις is the dative plural 'in the halls'.

sentences.t:
ἀμφότερον, κῦδός τε καὶ ἀγλαΐη καὶ ὄνειαρ,
δειπνήσαντας ἴμεν πολλὴν ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
In both ways, glory and splendour and benefit,
having dined to go over wide, boundless earth.
sentences.i: It is a glory and a splendour and a benefit alike for you to go on, after you have dined, over the wide, boundless earth.
sentences.n: The line has no verb of its own and hangs on the offer before it. ἀμφότερον is neuter, 'in both ways', and the three nouns κῦδος 'glory', ἀγλαΐη 'splendour' (from ἀγλαός 'splendid') and ὄνειαρ 'benefit, help' stand beside it. δειπνήσαντας is the aorist participle 'having dined', accusative plural because it goes with the unspoken subject of ἴμεν, the two guests, the epic infinitive of εἶμι 'go'. πολλὴν … ἀπείρονα γαῖαν is 'wide, boundless earth': ἀπείρων is 'boundless' (ἀ- + πεῖραρ 'limit'), and ἐπ’ is ἐπί with the accusative, 'over'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις τραφθῆναι ἀν’ Ἑλλάδα καὶ μέσον Ἄργος,
ὄφρα τοι αὐτὸς ἕπωμαι, ὑποζεύξω δέ τοι ἵππους,
ἄστεα δ’ ἀνθρώπων ἡγήσομαι·
sentences.i: And if you wish to travel round through Hellas and the middle of Argos, so that I may follow you myself, I will yoke the horses for you and lead you to the towns of men;
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις is 'but if you wish', the second offer. τραφθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of τρέπω 'turn', here 'to go about, make a journey round', and ἀνά is 'through'. Ἑλλάς and μέσον Ἄργος are named together; the Greek does not draw their boundaries, and Ἑλλάς is a region's name here. ὄφρα … ἕπωμαι is purpose, 'that I may follow' (ἕπομαι), with τοι 'you'. ὑποζεύξω is 'I shall yoke under' (compare ζεῦξον ὑφ’ ἅρματ’ at 47), τοι is 'for you' again, and ἡγήσομαι 'I shall lead'. ἄστεα ἀνθρώπων is 'the towns of men'.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἡμέας
αὔτως ἀππέμψει, δώσει δέ τι ἕν γε φέρεσθαι,
ἠέ τινα τριπόδων εὐχάλκων ἠὲ λεβήτων,
ἠὲ δύ’ ἡμιόνους ἠὲ χρύσειον ἄλεισον.
sentences.l:
and nobody us
just so will send away, but he will give some one thing, at least, to carry off,
either one of tripods of good bronze or of cauldrons,
or two mules or a golden goblet.”
sentences.i: and no one will send us away without more ado: he will give us at least one thing to carry off, either a tripod of good bronze, or a cauldron, or two mules, or a golden goblet.”
sentences.n: ἡμέας is the uncontracted accusative of ἡμεῖς 'us'. ἀππέμψει is ἀποπέμψει with the π doubled: 'will send away'. αὔτως, 'just so', here 'empty-handed, without more ado'. δώσει δέ τι ἕν γε φέρεσθαι is 'and he will give something, one thing at least, to carry away'. In the list, τινα governs the partitive genitives τριπόδων and λεβήτων, 'one of the tripods … or of the cauldrons'; εὐχάλκων is 'of good bronze'; ἡμιόνους are 'mules'; ἄλεισον is a goblet. The closing quotation mark ends Menelaus's speech.
